title: The Word Became Flesh; the First Disciples
summary: John opens with a prologue about the Word who was with God and was God in the beginning, through whom all things were made, and who became flesh and dwelt among us, full of grace and truth. John the Baptist then testifies that he is not the Christ but a voice preparing the way, and he points to Jesus as the Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world. Andrew, Simon Peter, Philip, and Nathanael begin to follow Jesus, who promises that they will see heaven opened.
story:
Matthew begins with Abraham, Mark with John the Baptist, and Luke with the births of John and Jesus. John begins before the world. His first words, “In the beginning”, repeat the first words of Genesis, and he tells us that the one about to walk onto the stage of history was there when the curtain first rose, as the Word through whom God made everything. The prologue (verses 1 to 18) gives the reader, in advance, the knowledge the characters in the story lack, so that every later scene is read with irony: the crowds argue about where Jesus comes from, and the reader already knows he comes from the Father's side.

Then the narrative starts, and it moves day by day (verses 29, 35, and 43 each open with “The next day”, and 2:1 continues with “On the third day”). One witness after another names who Jesus is: Lamb of God, Son of God (or God's Chosen One, in some manuscripts), Rabbi, Messiah, the one Moses wrote about, King of Israel, and finally, in Jesus' own words, Son of Man. Some interpreters count these days as an opening week that echoes the seven days of Genesis 1 and ends at the Cana wedding; others think the count is too uncertain to carry that weight. Either way the chapter lays out, at the start, nearly every title the Gospel will unfold, and it ends with a promise (verse 51) that the next chapters begin to keep.
historical:
John the Baptist was a well-known prophetic figure in his own right. The Jewish historian Josephus, writing his Jewish Antiquities around AD 93 to 94, describes him as a good man who urged Jews to practice virtue, justice toward one another, and piety toward God, and to come to baptism (Antiquities 18.116-119). Josephus says that Herod Antipas, the son of Herod the Great who ruled Galilee and Perea from 4 BC to AD 39, feared that John's influence over the crowds might lead to an uprising, and had him imprisoned and executed at the fortress of Machaerus, east of the Dead Sea. John's movement outlived him: Acts finds Apollos in Alexandria and a group of disciples in Ephesus who knew only the baptism of John (Acts 18:25, 19:1-7). If the Gospel was finished at Ephesus, as early tradition holds, its insistence that John was not the Light but a witness to it (verses 8, 15, 20) may speak to followers of the Baptist who still revered him.

The wilderness near the Jordan was charged with meaning. Isaiah 40:3 had pictured a road prepared in the wilderness for God's return. The community whose library was found at Qumran, a few miles from the Jordan's mouth, applied the same verse to itself: the Community Rule (1QS 8:13-14) explains the group's withdrawal to the desert as preparing the way of the Lord through study of the Law. The same scroll says its members would live by the first rules of the community until the coming of a prophet and the Messiahs of Aaron and Israel (1QS 9:11), and a small Qumran collection of proof texts, the Testimonia (4Q175), sets side by side Deuteronomy 18:18-19 (the prophet like Moses), Numbers 24:15-17 (the star from Jacob), and Deuteronomy 33:8-11 (the blessing of Levi). This is the world of expectation in which a delegation from Jerusalem asks John whether he is the Christ, Elijah, or the Prophet. Nothing in the Gospels shows that John belonged to the Qumran group, but the two shared a wilderness, a text, and a hope.

The places are real but not all can be pinned down. Bethany beyond the Jordan (verse 28) is not the Bethany near Jerusalem where Lazarus lived. Origen, who visited the region in the third century, could not find a Bethany on the river and argued in his Commentary on John (book 6) for the reading Bethabara, which then entered many later manuscripts. The site of Al-Maghtas at Wadi al-Kharrar, on the Jordanian bank, with churches and pilgrim buildings from the fourth century on, was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2015 under the name Bethany beyond the Jordan. Rainer Riesner (Tyndale Bulletin 38, 1987) proposed instead that John meant Batanea, the region east of the Sea of Galilee. Bethsaida (verse 44), home of Andrew, Peter, and Philip, lay near where the Jordan enters the Sea of Galilee; Josephus says the tetrarch Philip raised it to the status of a city and renamed it Julias (Antiquities 18.28). Its site is disputed between et-Tell and el-Araj. Nazareth is named nowhere in the Old Testament, in Josephus, or in the Mishnah and Talmud. The earliest mention of it outside Christian writings is a Hebrew inscription listing the priestly courses, found at Caesarea in 1962 and dated to the third or fourth century AD. Excavation shows a small farming village in Jesus' day, which helps explain Nathanael's question.
cultural:
Jewish hope in this period had no single fixed shape, and verses 19 to 25 show three figures a Jewish questioner might have in mind. The Christ or Messiah (both words mean anointed one; verse 41 gives the Aramaic-derived Messias and translates it) was the hoped-for king from David's line; the Psalms of Solomon 17, from the first century BC, pray for such a son of David to purge Jerusalem and rule in righteousness. Elijah, taken up alive in 2 Kings 2, was expected to return before the day of the Lord (Malachi 4:5), and Sirach 48:10 says he would restore the tribes of Jacob. The Prophet recalled Moses' promise that God would raise up a prophet like him (Deuteronomy 18:15), a figure the crowds in John 6:14 and 7:40 also discuss. John denies being any of them. When he calls himself a voice (Isaiah 40:3), he makes himself as small as possible: a sound that points and then fades.

The sandal remark in verse 27 would have been felt at once. A later rabbinic saying attributed to Rabbi Joshua ben Levi (third century) holds that a disciple should do for his teacher every task a slave does for his master except untying his sandal (Babylonian Talmud, Ketubbot 96a). If that attitude was already current, John is saying he is not fit to do for Jesus even the one task too low for a disciple. Disciples in this world attached themselves to a teacher, followed him on the road, and lived near him to learn a way of life. Rabbi, literally ‘my great one’, was a respectful address for a teacher, and the Gospel translates it for readers who did not know it (verse 38). The tenth hour (verse 39), counting from sunrise, was about four in the afternoon, late enough that the two disciples would have stayed the night. Cephas (verse 42) is the Aramaic kēpha, rock, rendered Petros in Greek; a new name in Scripture often marks a new calling (Abram to Abraham, Jacob to Israel). Sitting under one's own fig tree (verse 48) was a prophetic picture of peace and security (Micah 4:4, Zechariah 3:10).

The word logos, translated Word, reached Jewish and Greek readers differently. Jewish readers heard God's creative speech (“And God said” in Genesis 1; “By the word of the LORD the heavens were made”, Psalm 33:6), the word that came to the prophets, and the figure of Wisdom who was beside God at creation (Proverbs 8:22-31). Wisdom of Solomon 9:1-2 puts God's word and wisdom side by side as agents of creation, and Sirach 24:8 describes Wisdom being told to pitch her tent in Jacob, the same picture John uses in verse 14. The Aramaic Targums, the synagogue paraphrases of Scripture, often speak of the Memra (word) of the Lord acting where the Hebrew speaks of God himself; in Targum Neofiti to Genesis 1 it is the Memra of the Lord that creates, though the Targums in their present form are later than John and scholars debate how early this usage is. Philo of Alexandria, a Jewish philosopher who died around AD 50, called the Logos God's firstborn, the eldest of the angels, the Beginning, the name of God, and the man after God's image (On the Confusion of Tongues 146). For Greek readers shaped by Heraclitus and the Stoics, logos named the rational principle that orders the universe. John's prologue speaks to all these worlds and then says what none of them expected: the Word became flesh.
literary:
The prologue (verses 1 to 18) is carefully built prose with a poetic rhythm, and many scholars think it is shaped like a hymn or built on one. Its opening lines use a stair-step pattern in which the last key word of one clause becomes the first of the next: Word, God; life, light; light, darkness. The whole passage is framed by matching ends: the Word is with God (pros ton theon) in verse 1, and the one and only Son is at the Father's side, literally ‘into the bosom of the Father’, in verse 18; the Word is called God in both verses. Between those frames the prologue moves from eternity (verses 1 to 5), to John's witness (6 to 8), to the Light coming into a world that did not receive him (9 to 13), to the Word made flesh and the Son who makes the Father known (14 to 18). R. Alan Culpepper (New Testament Studies 27, 1980) argued that the passage is a chiasm, a mirrored arrangement, with its pivot at verse 12b, the right to become children of God. The prose sections about John (6 to 8 and 15) interrupt the poetry deliberately, tying eternity to a man with a name and a date.

After the prologue the chapter becomes narrative, and its governing word is testimony. The verb testify (martyreō) and the noun testimony (martyria) appear seven times in the chapter and are among the Gospel's favorite words, used some forty-seven times in all. The Baptist's section is built as a trial: officials interrogate, John answers with three denials that grow shorter (verses 20 and 21, ‘I am not the Christ’, ‘I am not’, ‘No’), and then he gives positive testimony twice (verses 29 to 34). The disciples' section is built as a chain: John points, two follow, Andrew finds Simon, Jesus finds Philip, Philip finds Nathanael. The verb find recurs, and the invitation “Come and see” is spoken first by Jesus (verse 39) and then by Philip (verse 46), so that the disciple repeats the Master's words. The titles climb as the chapter goes on, and Jesus closes the chapter by adding his own, Son of Man, introduced with the solemn double amen (Truly, truly), a formula found only in John in the New Testament and used there twenty-five times.

outline.t: The Word in the beginning: life and light
John, a witness to the Light
John's testimony: not the Christ, but a voice
Andrew and Simon Peter follow Jesus

doctrines.note: “The Word became flesh and made His dwelling among us” (verse 14) is the Bible's most direct statement of the incarnation. The eternal Word did not pretend to be human or merely indwell a man; he became flesh, a word John chose for full, frail human nature. The church's later confession at Chalcedon (451) of one person in two natures, truly God and truly human, is a careful restatement of this verse.

The Word was with God (distinct from the Father) and was God (sharing his nature) in verse 1. Verse 18 calls the Son “Himself God” at the Father's side (the earliest manuscripts read ‘one and only God’, others ‘one and only Son’), and verses 32 and 33 show the Spirit descending and remaining on him. The Nicene Creed (325, expanded 381) drew directly on this chapter's language.

“Through Him all things were made, and without Him nothing was made that has been made” (verse 3). John places the Son at the work of creation, echoing Genesis 1, and draws a hard line between the Maker and everything made. The one who redeems the world is the one who made it, which is why his coming is described as coming to his own (verse 11).

John the Baptist calls Jesus “the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world” (verse 29). The image gathers several Old Testament strands: the Passover lamb (Exodus 12), the lambs of the daily offering (Exodus 29:38-42), the lamb God provides in Genesis 22:8, and the servant of Isaiah 53:7 led like a lamb to slaughter. The singular sin and the scope, the world, point to a death that deals with sin itself.

Those who receive the Word are given the right to become children of God, “born not of blood, nor of the desire or will of man, but born of God” (verse 13). New birth is God's act, not a matter of ancestry, human effort, or human decision, a theme Jesus develops with Nicodemus in chapter 3.

words.note: Logos, word. In ordinary Greek it means a spoken word, a message, a reason, or an account, and it occurs about 330 times in the New Testament (forty times in John). BDAG, the standard lexicon, treats its use in John 1:1 and 1:14 as a separate sense: a title for the preexistent Son, used this way only in the prologue. It presents the Son as God's self-expression, the way a word expresses a speaker's mind, and it draws on both the Jewish and Greek backgrounds described above while claiming something neither held: this Word is a person, and he became flesh.

Skēnoō, to pitch a tent, to dwell. The Word made His dwelling among us, literally tented or tabernacled among us. The verb occurs only five times in the New Testament, here and four times in Revelation (7:15, 12:12, 13:6, 21:3), where God dwells with his people in the new creation. It recalls the tabernacle in the wilderness, where God's glory filled the tent (Exodus 40:34), and Sirach 24:8, where Wisdom pitches her tent in Jacob. The glory that once filled the tabernacle is now seen in the flesh of Jesus.

Monogenēs, one and only, unique. It occurs nine times in the New Testament, three times in Luke for an only child (7:12, 8:42, 9:38), once in Hebrews 11:17 for Isaac, the unique son of promise though not Abraham's only son, and five times in John's writings for the Son (John 1:14, 1:18, 3:16, 3:18, 1 John 4:9). Older translations, following the Latin unigenitus, rendered it only begotten. Many twentieth-century scholars argued it simply means unique, one of a kind; others, such as Charles Lee Irons (in Retrieving Eternal Generation, 2017), have defended the older sense of an only son born of a father. Either way Jesus is the Son in a sense no one else is, even though believers become children of God (verse 12).

Charis, grace, favor freely given. It occurs about 155 times in the New Testament, mostly in Paul, but only four times in John, all in the prologue (verses 14, 16, 17), and never again in the Gospel. Paired with truth in verses 14 and 17, it likely echoes the Hebrew pair hesed and emet in Exodus 34:6, God's loyal love and faithfulness. The phrase grace upon grace in verse 16 (charin anti charitos) is debated: it may mean grace piled on grace, or grace in place of grace, the new gift of Christ replacing the earlier gift of the law; verse 17 makes the second reading attractive to many.

Exēgeomai, to lead out, explain, tell in full. It occurs six times in the New Testament, the other five in Luke and Acts for reporting events in detail (Luke 24:35, Acts 10:8, 15:12, 15:14, 21:19). The related noun gives English its word exegesis. In verse 18 it is the last word of the prologue: no one has ever seen God, but the Son has made him known. Jesus is God's own explanation of himself.

Amnos, lamb. It occurs only four times in the New Testament (John 1:29, 1:36, Acts 8:32 quoting Isaiah 53:7, and 1 Peter 1:19), while Revelation uses a different word, arnion, some twenty-nine times for the Lamb who was slain. C. F. Burney and Joachim Jeremias proposed that behind it stands the Aramaic ṭalyā, which can mean both lamb and servant or child, linking the title to Isaiah's servant; the suggestion is possible but unproven.

Menō, to remain, stay, abide. It occurs about 118 times in the New Testament and forty times in John, more than any other book. In this chapter it is used both plainly and with depth: the Spirit descends and remains on Jesus (verses 32 and 33), and the disciples ask where he is staying and remain with him that day (verses 38 and 39). The same verb later carries Jesus' call to abide in him as branches in a vine (15:4-10). The first disciples' question about a lodging opens onto the Gospel's picture of lasting union with Christ.

christ:
Few chapters in the Bible say more about who Jesus is. He existed before creation, was with God and was God, and made all things. He is the life and light of humanity, the light the darkness could not overcome. He became flesh, a full human being, and dwelt among us, revealing the glory of God, full of grace and truth. That phrase echoes Exodus 34:6, where God proclaims himself “abounding in loving devotion and faithfulness” just after Moses had asked to see his glory and been told “no one can see Me and live” (Exodus 33:18-20). John's claim is that what Moses could not see has now been seen: “No one has ever seen God, but the one and only Son, who is Himself God and is at the Father's side, has made Him known” (verse 18). He is greater than Moses, not because the law was bad, but because the law was given through a servant while grace and truth came in person.

The Baptist adds three more strands. Jesus is the Lamb who takes away sin, an image the Gospel will close at the cross, where he dies at the hour of the Passover and not one of his bones is broken (19:36, echoing Exodus 12:46). He is the one on whom the Spirit rests, as Isaiah 11:2 promised of the shoot from Jesse, and he will baptize with the Holy Spirit, the gift he breathes on his disciples in 20:22. And he is the Son of God (or, in some manuscripts, God's Chosen One, recalling Isaiah 42:1, where God puts his Spirit on his chosen servant). The disciples then give him the titles of Israel's hope: Messiah, the one of whom Moses and the prophets wrote, King of Israel.

Jesus' final promise alludes to Jacob's dream at Bethel (Genesis 28:12), where angels went up and down a ladder between heaven and earth and Jacob called the place the house of God. Jesus says the angels will ascend and descend on the Son of Man, the figure of Daniel 7:13 who receives dominion from the Ancient of Days. He is the meeting place of heaven and earth, the true Bethel. Nathanael, a true Israelite in whom there is no deceit, stands in contrast to Jacob, whose name was bound up with deceit (Genesis 27:35-36), and he is promised a greater vision than Jacob's. The link to Genesis 28 is an allusion rather than a prediction: John reads the old story as a pattern that finds its fullness in Jesus.
interpretation:
The prologue has been among the most interpreted passages of the Bible from the second century on. The earliest known commentary on any Gospel, by Heracleon, a Valentinian teacher active around AD 170, began with John and survives only in fragments quoted by Origen, whose own vast Commentary on John, begun in Alexandria before he moved to Caesarea around 231, answers him point by point. Irenaeus of Lyon (Against Heresies, around 180) used verse 14 against teachers who denied that the Word truly took flesh. In the fourth-century Arian controversy both sides appealed to this chapter: Arius's followers read the Word as the first and highest creature, while Athanasius (Orations against the Arians) and the Council of Nicaea (325) confessed the Son as of one substance with the Father. The punctuation of verses 3 and 4 became part of that fight, as noted under the text. John Chrysostom preached eighty-eight homilies on John at Antioch around 390, and Augustine preached 124 tractates on it at Hippo in the early fifth century. In his Confessions (7.9) Augustine records that he found in the books of the Platonists something like “In the beginning was the Word”, but not that the Word became flesh and dwelt among us. That contrast has shaped Christian reading ever since.

Jewish interpreters of the Hebrew Bible did not comment on John, but Jewish tradition bears on the chapter at two points. Genesis Rabbah 68:12 records a dispute between Rabbi Hiyya and Rabbi Yannai over whether the angels in Jacob's dream went up and down on the ladder or on Jacob himself, a reading that makes Jesus' words in verse 51 striking. In modern scholarship Daniel Boyarin (Harvard Theological Review 94, 2001) has argued that the Logos theology of the prologue belongs within a Jewish stream of thought about God's Word or Memra that the rabbis later rejected, while Alan Segal's Two Powers in Heaven (1977) traced rabbinic polemic against such ideas.

Medieval readers took the prologue as the summit of Scripture. Thomas Aquinas's Lectures on John (around 1270) treat it with the full apparatus of scholastic theology, and the tradition gave John the eagle as his symbol (Augustine, Harmony of the Gospels 1.6), because he soars highest. Luther's 1522 Preface to the New Testament ranked John above the other Gospels for its record of Jesus' words, and Calvin's commentary (1553) called it the key that opens the others. Goethe's Faust (Part One, 1808) has its hero translate verse 1 as Word, then Mind, then Power, and finally Deed. Rudolf Bultmann's commentary (1941) argued that the prologue adapted a pre-Christian Gnostic hymn from Baptist circles, a thesis even his students did not accept. C. H. Dodd (The Interpretation of the Fourth Gospel, 1953) and Raymond Brown (Anchor Bible, 1966) read it against Jewish Wisdom and the Old Testament, which is now the majority view.

In worship the prologue is the Gospel for Christmas Day in the Western lectionaries, and in the Orthodox churches John 1:1-17 is read at the Paschal Divine Liturgy, often in many languages. From the late Middle Ages until the reforms that followed the Second Vatican Council, the Roman Mass ended with the Last Gospel, John 1:1-14, the priest genuflecting at the words ‘and the Word was made flesh’. The Baptist's words in verse 29 became the Agnus Dei, which the Liber Pontificalis says Pope Sergius I (687-701) ordered sung at the breaking of the bread. In art, Matthias Grünewald's Isenheim Altarpiece (about 1512 to 1516) shows John the Baptist beside the cross with a long pointing finger and a lamb at his feet; Karl Barth kept a reproduction over his desk as a picture of what theology is for. The Tudor composer John Sheppard set Verbum caro factum est for choir, and the Revised Common Lectionary reads verses 29 to 42 and 43 to 51 on the second Sunday after Epiphany in years A and B.
text:
Several differences between English Bibles in this chapter come from the manuscripts.

Verse 18 is the most important. The earliest papyri, P66 (about AD 200) and P75 (late second or early third century), and the fourth-century codices Sinaiticus and Vaticanus read monogenēs theos, ‘the one and only God’ or ‘the only begotten God’. Codex Alexandrinus (fifth century), most later Greek manuscripts, and the Latin tradition read ho monogenēs huios, ‘the only begotten Son’, the reading behind the King James Version. Modern critical editions (Nestle-Aland, the United Bible Societies, and the SBL Greek New Testament) print theos, and most modern versions follow, rendering it ‘the one and only Son, who is himself God’ (as the BSB does) or ‘God the only Son’ (ESV). The Son reading is smoother and matches 3:16 and 3:18, which is one reason critics think scribes changed God to Son rather than the reverse.

Verses 3 and 4 have no punctuation in the oldest manuscripts, so editors must decide where the words ‘that has come into being’ belong. Taken with verse 3, the text reads as in most English Bibles. Taken with verse 4, it reads ‘what has come into being in him was life’, which is how most second- and third-century writers read it and how the Nestle-Aland text punctuates it. When fourth-century Arians used the second reading to argue that the Spirit was a created thing, orthodox writers such as Chrysostom preferred the first, and most translations still do. Verse 13 is plural (those who were born) in every Greek manuscript, but Tertullian and some Old Latin witnesses read the singular, ‘who was born’, applying it to Jesus' virgin birth; no modern version adopts it.

In verse 34 nearly all manuscripts read ‘the Son of God’, but the first hand of Codex Sinaiticus, one or two early papyri, and some Old Latin and Old Syriac witnesses read ‘the Chosen One of God’. The SBL Greek New Testament and the NIV (2011) adopt the Chosen One, on the principle that scribes were more likely to change an unusual title to the familiar one; the ESV, NRSV, and BSB keep Son of God. In verse 28 the Textus Receptus, and so the King James Version, read Bethabara, following Origen's conjecture described above. In verse 42 later manuscripts and the KJV read ‘Simon the son of Jona’ where the earliest read ‘son of John’. In verse 51 the KJV's ‘Hereafter ye shall see’ reflects a word (ap' arti, from now on) that the earliest manuscripts lack.

teach.big: The eternal Word who made the world has become flesh, and in him the unseen God is made known, so that all who receive him become children of God and find in him the meeting place of heaven and earth.

outline.t: Before anything else existed, the Word was with God and was God; all life and light come from him, and darkness cannot defeat him.
God's pattern is to send witnesses who point away from themselves; John is great precisely because he is not the Light.
The Maker came to his own world and people and was refused, yet everyone who receives him is born of God, not by ancestry or effort.
God's answer to the ache to see him is not a vision but a person: the Word became flesh, full of grace and truth, and makes the Father known.
John's refusal of every title shows what faithful witness looks like: he is only a voice, and the One who matters is already standing among them.
John names Jesus the Lamb who bears away the world's sin and the Spirit-bearer who will baptize with the Spirit.
Following Jesus begins with his question, ‘What do you want?’, and his invitation to come and see, and it spreads from brother to brother.
Honest doubt is met, not scolded: Jesus knows Nathanael before they meet and promises him a greater sight than Jacob's, heaven opened on the Son of Man.

teach.pitfalls:
Three misreadings are common. The first treats the prologue as abstract philosophy and the logos as a Greek idea John borrowed, which misses how thoroughly the passage is rooted in Genesis, Exodus, and Jewish Wisdom, and how it ends not in an idea but in flesh. The second reads verse 1 as if the Word were simply the Father under another name, or as a lesser god; the text holds together distinction (with God) and full deity (was God), and teachers should keep both halves. The third turns verses 12 and 13 into a sermon on human decision alone. The verse does speak of receiving and believing, but it insists that the new birth is God's doing, and preaching should hold both without forcing a later debate onto John.

With the narrative, avoid treating Nathanael's fig tree as a code for something secret he was doing; the text does not say, and the point is that Jesus knew him. Avoid using ‘the Jews’ in verse 19 as a label for Jewish people generally, since it names the Jerusalem authorities who sent the delegation. And do not turn verses 40 to 46 into an evangelism program: the pattern of one person bringing another is real, but the emphasis falls on Jesus, who asks the first question, finds Philip, and knows Nathanael before anyone speaks.
teach.pastoral: This chapter speaks gently to the doubter. Nathanael's scorn for Nazareth is not rebuked but answered with an invitation and then with evidence that he was already known, and teachers can present the chapter as an open door for skeptics in the room. It also speaks to people who feel unseen or unwanted, including those whose family of origin failed them: verses 12 and 13 say that belonging to God's family does not depend on blood or a parent's will. Be careful not to imply that earthly families do not matter; the point is that no one is shut out of God's family by the one they were born into.

hard.q: Does John 1:1 say the Word was ‘a god’, and can a Jewish monotheist say the Word was God at all?
hard.a:
The objection comes in two forms. The grammatical form is that the last clause places the noun God first and gives it no article, literally ‘God was the Word’, and that a noun without the article should be translated as indefinite. The New World Translation of the Jehovah's Witnesses (1950) accordingly reads ‘the Word was a god’, and Jason BeDuhn, a scholar of religion at Northern Arizona University, defended that rendering as the most literal in Truth in Translation (2003). The historical form is sharper. Israel's confession is “The LORD our God, the LORD is One” (Deuteronomy 6:4), and Jewish readers from antiquity to today have heard the worship of Jesus as a breach of it; the rabbis later condemned belief in ‘two powers in heaven’, a polemic Alan Segal traced in detail (1977). Critical scholars such as Bart Ehrman (How Jesus Became God, 2014) argue that John's high view of Jesus is a late development, not what Jesus or his first followers believed.

On the grammar, most Greek scholars of every persuasion reject the indefinite reading. E. C. Colwell (1933) showed that definite predicate nouns placed before the verb usually lack the article, and Philip Harner (Journal of Biblical Literature 92, 1973) argued that such nouns most often describe quality or nature. On that reading the clause means that the Word had the full nature of God, what God was the Word was, without saying that the Word is the same person as the Father, who is the God the Word was with in the previous clause. Bruce Metzger (Theology Today, 1953) and Daniel Wallace (Greek Grammar Beyond the Basics, 1996) make the same case, and they note that John uses God without the article in verses 6, 12, 13, and 18 of this chapter for the one true God. On the history, Richard Bauckham (Jesus and the God of Israel, 2008) and Larry Hurtado (Lord Jesus Christ, 2003) argue that the earliest Christians, all Jewish monotheists, included Jesus within the identity of Israel's one God from the start, for example by giving him the role of creator, which Jewish monotheism reserved for God alone. Daniel Boyarin, writing as a Jewish scholar, argues that ideas of a divine Word alongside God were at home in first-century Judaism before the rabbis ruled them out. The church confesses what the verse teaches: the Word is distinct from the Father and fully God, one God and not two. The Jewish objection is sincere and ancient and deserves a patient answer.

hard.q: In this chapter the Baptist and the first disciples recognize Jesus at once, but in the other Gospels recognition is slow. Can both be true?
hard.a:
The objection is strong. In John 1 the Baptist calls Jesus the Lamb of God and Son of God, and within days Andrew announces that he has found the Messiah and Nathanael calls Jesus Son of God and King of Israel. In Mark, Peter's confession, “You are the Christ” (Mark 8:29), comes halfway through the story as a turning point, and Jesus repeatedly silences those who would name him, a feature William Wrede called the messianic secret (1901). In Matthew 11:3 the Baptist, now in prison, sends to ask “Are You the One who was to come, or should we look for someone else?” John's Baptist also denies being Elijah (verse 21), while Jesus in Matthew 11:14 says “he is the Elijah who was to come.” David Friedrich Strauss (The Life of Jesus, 1835) and many later critics concluded that John rewrote the story to make Jesus' identity plain from the first page.

Responses fall into several groups. C. H. Dodd (Historical Tradition in the Fourth Gospel, 1963) argued that John's Baptist material rests on early tradition independent of the other Gospels, and scholars such as Craig Blomberg (The Historical Reliability of John's Gospel, 2001) and Craig Keener argue that first recognitions and later confessions are compatible: disciples could use titles like Messiah early and still need years, and a cross, to learn what they meant, which is exactly what happens to Peter in Mark 8:31-33. The Baptist's question from prison can be read as perplexity about what kind of Messiah Jesus was proving to be, not ignorance of who he was. On Elijah, many note that John denies being Elijah returned in person, while Luke 1:17 says he came “in the spirit and power of Elijah,” and Jesus speaks of his role. Others, including Raymond Brown, grant that John has shaped his material from a post-Easter vantage point, as the Gospel itself admits (2:22, 12:16), and argue that this is interpretation of history rather than invention. How much of the difference is arrangement and how much is perspective remains debated among scholars who hold a high view of Scripture.
